utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There was an issue in relation to P2550, which was marked for identification, I think. The issue was whether this document should be admitted under seal. The final conclusion of the parties, and going back to this, to the origin of this document, it turns out that it should be admitted under seal. Therefore, this document, which was MFI'd, is now admitted under seal. Yes. That is now on the record. Is the Gotovina Defence ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I did advise your courtroom officer as well as Mr. Monkhouse and the Prosecution of a concern I have with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About -- yes, I was informed that it might be necessary that I ask him to repeat my words if it comes to the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, and out of respect to the witness, I don't know if that is the case, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Gotovina Defence will call Pero Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perkovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. For that purpose, I would like to invite you to repeat the words as I speak them. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perkovic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, could you state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Pero Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where do you reside?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: In Vodice, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, prior to and after Operation Storm in August of 1995, were you a member of the 15th Home Guards Regiment?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to talk to but a few matters concerning the period of time before and after Operation Storm. But while you were in the 15th Home Guard Regiment, were you ever given an order to commit a crime?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you ever given an order specifically to burn a Serb house, or to loot a home, or to mistreat civilians?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: While you were in the 15th Home Guards Regiment, were you warned not to commit such actions?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: During the operation we had in Skradin, since that was our starting point in Operation Storm, we were ordered to take care of civilians, to have them as far away from any harm as possible. That was done by our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was that commander?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Ivo Porusic. He commanded the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'd like them, for the record, to be noted that the witness has referred to some papers that he pulled out of his pocket, so I think that should be clear on the record, and we should have a chance to examine this and ask the witness -- perhaps he should be asked now what those are and when they were created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Perkovic, although I missed it, apparently you have taken some papers. Could you tell us what you have now in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before me I have the names of the commanders in my battalion, the name of my platoon and company, because so many years have gone by that I no longer remember the name of the battalion commander. I could get confused easily, and therefore I took this aide-memoire with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when did you create that document? When did you write down -- or did you write them down yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I made the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe. And please do not consult these notes without asking for permission, so if you would just not read names in answer to any question, and if you do not know the name, tell that you don't know it anymore but that it may refresh your memory if you consult the document you produced yourself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, we have not seen these notes nor have we told the witness to prepare them so that the officer knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that became sufficiently clear from the last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Perkovic, you were accused -- were you accused with other members of your regiment for committing crimes after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I was accused of a murder of Serb civilians in the village of Gosici, along with a few other individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when were you arrested, sir, do you recall, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in October, once I came back from the front lines. I no longer remember the exact date. It may have been early October or mid-October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you arrested by the military police, the civilian police, or both?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: It was early in the morning, and I think both types of police were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thereafter, were you questioned by the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, if I could bring up 65 ter 1D2728 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Perkovic, this is the Official Note of your interview that we discussed last night, and it is a dated 16 October 1995 by the Zadar-Knin police administration crime police department. Now, at the outset it has your nickname as Matilda. Is that a nickname or an alias that you used?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a bar called Matilda, and I guess that's why I got the nickname Matilda. They asked me for a nickname, and I told them I didn't have any, and then they said, What do you mean? Of course you do, you're Matilda. And then I put two and two together and realized that the nickname was after the bar I owned in Vodice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if we could scroll down to the bottom of this page, and it notes during the course of this interview that during this time: "While he was out on the ground, the following people were always with him." I'd like to talk to you just before we get to that about the statement that you make below -- above that during the course of the interviews. And it notes in this interview that: "Having returned from their leave, his unit went to Rudele, where they covered two locations, each time three days (3 X 3 shifts). At this location he took an automobile, a white Zastava 102 [sic], without licence plates from the garage of a house?" Now the white Zastava that you took that had been -- tell us about that. Was that a vehicle that had been left behind by someone who left the area?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: There were many such cars there abandoned. This one was a white Zastava passenger car, and I simply took it, since, at that time, I did not have a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The car did not belong to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: It did not. It was an abandoned vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page of the English and the -- I believe it is the second page of the B/C/S, at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Talking about the people in your unit who you say were almost always with you. And the last person on that list is an individual by the name of Ivica Petric. How long had you known Ivica Petric?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him since 1991, the beginning of the war and throughout. Before the war, I had not known him since he was quite younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the time when you knew him, Mr. Perkovic, did you become aware that he had had numerous arrests and problems with the law?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that. The story among the soldiers was that he was a drug addict and several over things, but I don't know whether any of that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about his drug problem. Did you discuss or learn -- did you discuss the drug problem with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand the relevance of asking about the drug problem of a witness, on the Defence witness list that has not been called yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The witness list, I mean, it will become evident as we go through here, who these people are, where they are, their involvement with one another. I think counsel has gone through these statements and knows full well how they all tie together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection about relevance is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The question I asked you, did you discuss or did you learn about Mr. Petric's drug problem?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I never discussed that with him, but certain people at the Home Guards Unit discussed that. I no longer remember who it was that was talking about him. In any case, one couldn't notice anything on him, because he was a good soldier, and it was not noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you say he was a good soldier. He was not an active soldier prior to being mobilized the day before Operation Storm, was he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we try to put the questions in such a way that can be avoided, because this is really something you could expect, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was Petric an active member of a military unit prior to being mobilized before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was in the reserve force of the 15th Home Guard Regiment, before the Storm. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your statement in the prior page, you say that he, among others, was almost always with him. Is that true, that Ivica Petric was almost always with you?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. We were only together in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, staying on this list, and if we could stay on this page for the English, but if we could just flip back to the prior page in the B/C/S. And I want to ask you about an individual by the name of Nikola Rasic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I do. He had been my commander back in 1991. He commanded my platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Zec, rabbit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let me just try to understand. You ask the witness, You say in your statement that Petric was always with you, and then the witness said, No, that's wrong. It was only when I was out on the field. Now, if you look at the statement, it says, During this time, while he was out on the ground, the following people were always with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say -- you stated that, He was always with you, isn't it? That's not true. It was only when I was out in the field. That's exactly what he said, so you misquote him, ask him whether it's correct, then he says it is not correct, and then he gives the right quote. So a rather useless exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I will be as precise as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this individual, Mr. Rasic, was he convicted -- was he charged or convicted of committing any crimes?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, he was convicted of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did he do?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: He was convicted because he wounded an old woman. I think he used a side-arm. He fired at her and wounded her in the face. The trial was in Zadar, and he got a prison sentence of one and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now another person you have on this list is Zvonimir Lasan. He is also on this list as -- as Mr. President correctly points out, that was almost [sic] with you when you were out on the field. Mr. Lasan, you're familiar with him as well, are you?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was with us in our platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he have any aliases or nicknames?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We called him Laso.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was also -- was he -- pardon me. Was he convicted of committing any crimes?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: He [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] got six years for the murder of a Serb civilian in a village where we were not on mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, going back to Mr. Rasic for a second, the conviction he got for, you say, shooting the woman in the jaw, was that a Serb civilian as well?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Another person have here is a Miso Jakovljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just at line -- page 10, line 22 in the transcript, it says: "I got six years." I think the witness said he got six years. I think that is fairly important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Miso Jakovljevic, are you familiar with that man?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. For a while he was with us, in a counter-sabotage platoon and at the regiment for a while as well. But on both occasions it was for short periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he have any nicknames, sir?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Core.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the next person you have I'd like to ask you about is, do you know an individual who is not on this list whose name is Nedeljko Mijic?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I know him. He was with us in the platoon. He was a suspect in the case of the murder of Serb civilians in the village of Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was -- do you know him by the nickname Zuki?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anybody refer to him as Nedjo?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, just Zuki. That's what they called him when we were in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, staying with your witness statement and -- to the civilian police, I'd just like to ask you a question in the middle of the English, and it should be the next page in the B/C/S, it says that: "Moreover he stated" - this being you - "stated that in Kistanje he found a Ciganka AP, a Winchester rifle, a Skorpion automatic weapon. And in the area of Zrmanja he found a 12-calibre hunting rifle, and he also stated that he had four ... grenades and a Zolja rocket-launcher at home?" Now, the weapons that you found in Kistanje, are these weapons that you found searching houses in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was found on that occasion. The hand-grenades and the Zolja is was what I was issued with. As for the other weapons, I came across those while searching the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm having a concern about the leading. I mean, this is direct examination. He should be asked -- without showing him a previous statement should be asked, you know, what weapons you found in Kistanje, if any? We've established the police station. The evidence of the witness should not be based on the prior statement recorded by someone, because I think that is highly leading. The purpose of direct examination is to elicit the witness's evidence, and then if he needs his memory to be refreshed or if he can't remember, then it is a separate issue. But to start off, to read a portion of it, and then to ask the witness -- and use it as foundation for your next question, I think that is improper, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Prosecution did that for over a year in various and numerous instances, not just with their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was always objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Often it was. There was a kind of a general guidance from this Chamber that, that examination-in-chief, and even in cross, that it was preferable, first, to ask a witness and only then take him to a document. It -- the guidance is still valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I may, Mr. President, I will follow Your Honours' guidance. This was not done with Official Notes repeatedly by the Prosecution. But I will follow Your Honours' guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In Kistanje, Mr. Perkovic, did soldiers -- or in other villages did soldiers find weapons in various locations that were being searched?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: There was quite a lot of weapons in different houses, left behind after they had fled. They simply left the weapons behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say "they," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Serb soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you found these weapons in Kistanje, and when you were in Kistanje, did you see any burning going on in Kistanje, sir?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Seldom. Perhaps one or two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know who did that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to talk to you about an incident in Cakici. Now, when did you first get to Cakici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We came for the first time to the village of Cakici after the operation in the village of Kistanje. We were mopping up the terrain around the villages near the Zrmanja. And then as we were moving towards the Zrmanja we turned to the Cakici, the village of Cakici. Otherwise, our forces were never in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did you -- who did you go to Cakici with the first time?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Perhaps Petric and Zec, Zuki, Lasan were with me. A couple of others. I don't remember any other names. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you go in a military vehicle, or did you go in a civilian car?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. We had a camouflage van used by our platoon. I don't know whether we used that one or a civilian vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go to third to bottom paragraph in the English. I believe it's on the same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The first time he was in Cakici was about ten days after the start of the operation. At the time he was in the company of Goran Babac, Zvonimir Lasan, Ivica Petric, and Nikola Rasic. He cannot remember what car they went in, but he believes it was a civilian car."

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. What happened at the police was an interrogation where an admission was forced out of me, which had nothing to do with the truth. I wanted to cut their mistreatment short, so I made statements which had nothing to do with the truth or the actual situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what did you go to Cakici for?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Cakici sits right by the road. It was out of sheer curiosity that we went there to see if there was anybody there, any Serb soldiers. Before proceeding to the Zrmanja, we stopped by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you stop by and visit anybody?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: There was an elderly man -- or, rather, two relatives and a daughter; they lived in the village. And there was an old woman there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you begin to socialise with the woman that was there?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: She was a young woman, maybe 25, 27, or close to 30. Her father, or a relative of hers, I don't recall who he was, we became friends. We asked them if they required anything. They told us they didn't have cooking stove or any coffee, and we brought them some later on, and we would stop by to see how they were fairing on our way to the Zrmanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, did you go back to Cakici sometime after this first visit?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We would go back there. I think I was there three times in all. There was a car in Cakici. I don't know who it was who asked me to take the car. We went back there, and I helped tow the car out of village. I don't recall if it was Petric or Ladovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you went back and took a car and towed the car with Petric and Ladovic. Was it their car?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't their car. It was an abandoned vehicle, just as that Stojadin of mine was, or, rather, not mine, belonging to another ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Perkovic, where you learned that an old man had been killed in Cakici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I did. Once we came to visit the woman, her father, and that individual, the father was frightened and crying out of fear. He knew my name by that time and said to me, Pero, this neighbour of ours was killed. I went to see if this was true, and I did indeed find him lying on the ground in his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to that, did you have a discussion with other members of your unit that someone had been left behind to sleep in Cakici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard of anyone sleeping in Cakici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us put this in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in the English, and I do believe it's the next page in the B/C/S as well. The English would be the second to the top paragraph starting with: "Not long after ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can get some assistance from my colleague, the way this is in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're just continuing. Why not ask the witness, for example, whether he had any conversation with one of his mates, indicating that perhaps something would have happened to any of the people in that village. You just read again, you don't say you read, but that's what you are doing. Specific language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- very specific for the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will ask the question as Your Honour wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with any of the members of your units indicating that something had happened in the village, Cakici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't know that it had happened. It was only when I came to the village of Cakici that I learned that the old man had been killed. I didn't talk to anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's why I'm going back to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the -- your statement to the police, you noted that: "Not long after that, several days later, Petric and he saw Zec, Lasan, and Koro in a brown Renault 4 on the Djevrska-Knin road. They stopped on the road and asked one another where they were going. At that point, somebody from the Renault 4 said that they had 'left one, a man behind to sleep.' The three in the Renault 4 continued towards Kistanje, and the four of them set off for Cakici in Petric's green Stojadin." Now, did you tell the police that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't tell this to the police because I didn't know that this had happened on the ground. I heard this information at trial, while I was in the courtroom, the statement that you have just read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your trial was when, sir?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: My trial took place in the course of the nine months that I spent in prison, beginning in September. Of course, the trial didn't commence right away. We were first in detention, and then, in the course of these nine months, the trial took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The trial was after you gave these statements to the police, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't give this statement to the police, the one that you read out a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Cakici, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: When I got to Cakici, I found the old man and his daughter in tears. He said, Someone killed ... he didn't say who did that, and I didn't know who had killed the man, the old man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you go see the body?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The body was on the ground upstairs in the house. Of course, I felt sorry for the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see how he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think by a bullet in the forehead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there was a -- was there an investigation and trial concerning this killing?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Zadar, at the time the Varivode and Gosici was under way, Lasan was tried for the murder and sentenced to six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was -- was that Zvonimir Lasan?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zvonimir Lasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn our attention to the period of time that you were in Zrmanja. By the way, sir, before we leave Cakici, after you had gone on that occasion and seen the body, did you ever go back to Cakici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at a later date. During the trial, I saw that Core Jakovljevic, and Zec went there, and that they took the father and the girl to Sibenik. I don't know the reasons behind it or anything. I heard it during the trial. I didn't go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you learn the identity of the man who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I knew the name, but I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the man's house who had been killed, do you know if his house, after he was killed, had been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was set on fire. I went there once again, and I saw that the house had been set on fire. I don't know if the body was inside at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you learn, in conversation with other members of your unit, who set that house on fire?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, pardon that minor interruption, I just want to move ahead now to the period of time in Zrmanja, and just talking about that a bit. And with regard to Zrmanja, was there an incident when you and other members of your unit went to Zrmanja and took weapons from an old Serb man?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We got -- got to a village there which is the general area of Zrmanja, and we got across an old man whom we asked if he had any weapons. We asked about his son, and he said that his son had been a member of the Serb army. We then asked him, Are there any weapons to be found? And he said no. Next, Zec or somebody else, I don't recall correctly, took the man and tied him to a tree. They placed cloths about him and threatened that they would set him on fire unless he admitted to having weapons. I asked them, I pleaded with them to stop, and they untied him. We had a sip of brandy with the man. Later on I chatted with him for a while, and that was it. The old man had two cows and promised to give us a calf. We said that he -- we would be visiting him the following day, since we would be going back. The following day, since we were going back from the field in the Zrmanja, we wouldn't be sleeping. While on the ground in the search operations, we returned to his place. He wasn't there. He left a message for us behind: I left with the lambs; there is no calf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's -- before we get to that --

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There was an old lady, his neighbour, residing there as well, and we asked her, I believe her name was Marta, what had become of the old man, and she said that he had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us go back to the incident with Zec, you, and Lasan, where you were asking this old man for these weapons. Did you give you the weapons?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to page 4 in the English of, I believe -- towards the second-to-last paragraph, scrolling down, beginning at second-to-last paragraph about seven lines from the bottom. "Then Lasan and Zec tied the old man to the iron railing on the terrace and set some rags around him on fire. Right after that, the old man told them he had a rifle, so they untied him, and the old man took them to a forest just above the house where he showed them two rifles."

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a different case altogether. That old man was subsequently killed by Petric or this other individual, I don't know. I wasn't present there. I was present when they tied the old man to the railing, whereupon the old man took us to the forest, retrieved the rifle, which I took away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us talk about the instance where the old man was killed by Petric first. Now, in that instance did you or the other people in your unit tell you that this old man had found weapons and he had given them to you, or he had weapons and had given them to you?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We were going back from this old man's place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If the witness understood the question, I mean, I was a little confused. The witness just testified about not seeing the killing and then he got the weapons. And now the question is, Were you told by yourself or by other people what the old man had found weapons and had given them to you -- or he had weapon and has given them to you. We already said that he went to the forest and got the weapons, so I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would assist the Chamber if you would go step by step, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After this old man showed you these weapons, did you then talk to Petric?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: When the old man gave us the weapons, we went back to the location where I -- where our unit was present. Petric was walking towards us with this other individual who was also a suspect, and when we asked them about the weapons, they said that it was the old man who had given them weapons. Subsequently, we heard that a murder had taken place there. The commander was furious about it. The story was that an old man had been killed, and we presumed that it was that old man because he was the only one in the close proximity of where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did Petric tell that you he did it?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't. I heard that during the trial that Petric and this other individual were charged with this. I don't recall this other man's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you saying you don't recall the other man's name besides Petric who was charged with this?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Hrustic. I just remembered, Hrustic. I don't know his first name; I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you just say that you learned about this information during the trial of Petric on this killing?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about the killing while we were at the Zrmanja. But we didn't know who killed him. Petric got six years for that. But he shifted the blame on to the other, because they were blaming each other. They claimed that they had shot past the old man. At any rate, Petric got six years of imprisonment for that killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this individual?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Which individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The individual that was killed.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the family name was Canak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would that be Djuradj Canak?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just referring -- we don't need to get into this because the witness hasn't seen it, but to refer Your Honour and counsel to D918 of the identity of that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when this individual was killed, were you present when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I told you that when we were on our way back, we met Petric who was on his way to that place, whilst we were going back to our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me bring up 65 ter 1D2727, if I may. And while I'm doing that, Your Honour, if I could tender 65 ter 1D2728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness testified that that statement was not the truth, that it was forced out of him. I don't know if that is a matter -- I leave it the Chamber's hand if that is a matter of weight rather than admissibility. But that is what the evidence of the witness is on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly it is a matter of weight, Your Honour. Your Honour will take all this information into account as to what weight it will be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1539.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The objection is denied, to the extent it was an objection. Please proceed. Before we continue, perhaps I could ask one clarifying question. You said you were not present when that individual was killed. You were on your way back, when you met Petric, who was on his way to that place. You were going back to your units. Where was your unit at that specific time; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not far from the scene of crime. Our unit was deployed there because we were sweeping the area. It was maybe 200 or 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where were you stationed? In a house, in a school, in tents, in ... could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were in a yard, in a courtyard, from where we would go around the houses, sweeping the general area. That was our assembly point during the day, that particular yard, and at night, we would be going back to where we were stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where were you stationed at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my home, in Vodice. We didn't go back to the barracks. We never spent the night in the barracks. We would be going back to our homes, and the sweeping operations took place only during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were sleeping at home. And during the day, you were in your unit doing the sweeping operations. Could you tell us for how long a period at that moment such a -- such sweeping operations would take. Would it be five consecutive days, one day, ten days, 14 days? Could you give us an indication as how this was organised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, the mopping up started from Kistanje and then Rudele, and it may have lasted a week, seven days. Perhaps a bit more; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before going home, did you first report back to the yard where you were all gathered, before going home again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We would assemble there at the end of the day and go back home together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you then report to your command there, or what happened at the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Once the sweeping operation was over for the day, we would gather and go home collectively. Sometimes we would drop by Cakici on our way home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- but was there in that yard, was there a commander? Was a command ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our battalion commander was there with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ante Belak. He learned about the murder of the old man and was furious at that sort of conduct. I don't know what he did as a follow-up in that particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you gathered there in the mornings, was this Ante Belak the person who said, You go there, you go there, gave the instructions, gave the orders, where to go and what to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We got to the village of Zrmanja consisting of several hamlets. We wouldn't be specifically told where to go. We merely spread out and then at some point came back to the assembly point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was exactly then your task? I mean, what did that mean, search or mopping-up operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mopping-up operation was aimed at ensuring that there were no enemy soldiers left lurking and to search for weapons. Primarily it was aimed at finding any remaining Serb soldiers. That's what the main objective of the mopping-up or the sweeping operation, was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did any of the members of your unit, during that approximately a week, did they find any enemy soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw certain individuals who were killed, one or two, and they were covered with quicklime. I saw the individual as we were going back by the roadside, I don't know if it was the body of a civilian or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you report this back to your commander, what you had seen, that you were uncertain about whether you saw the bodies of civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were passing by in a car, and what I described was what we were able to glean out of the window in movement. I saw this one body covered with lime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I'd like to show you an individual that you previously noted, a Mr. Rasic, with the name of Zec --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I know we haven't heard the question yet, but I have even more concerns now about showing him the note of someone else. I don't know if the matter was put to the witness or not. But, I mean, if it was, was the answer clear? I mean, the purpose of showing him something is either to contradict something or to ask him to clarify or to ask him if he agrees with it. In all cases, it would be leading. Whatever Mr. Kehoe intends to do with this document, the matter should be elicited from the witness, and only if his answer is that he does not recall should a document be shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put on notice that you could expect. But we do not know what your question will be, and as I earlier said, we can listen to the question, but before putting it on the screen, perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, and we just e-mailed to Your Honour, as well as the OTP, any number of instances during the Zganjer direct examination where the MUP statements Official Notes were shown and used as the leaping-off point of questions so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But wasn't it -- is it my recollection that he, as a professional, had to deal with those notes in his official capacity, and he was not the one who provided the information. So the comparison is -- well, quite inventive, if I could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I can certainly ask this witness about Official Notes coming from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this witness never had to deal with Official Notes in his professional capacity. That's quite a difference. But please proceed, Mr. Kehoe. Let's not enter into an endless debate. I think that I gave guidance before. This is about the substance of these notes by someone who, apparently, has some personal knowledge on the basis of his own observations, or has not, and that's what we expect you to ask the witness about. And if their answers create a need to further look at the documents, we'll have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, just turning to this document, were aware that Mr. Rasic was interviewed in -- on the 12th October, 1995, about the particular incident where this old man was killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly. Turning to this document, Mr. Kehoe, that is exactly what Mr. Hedaraly was objecting against, and that now you say, turning to this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could turn your attention to page 10154, where Your Honour, Mr. President, led Mr. Buhin [phoen] through an MP note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was his own note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was his own note. Don't point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you should wait until Mr. Kehoe has finished. I'll have a look at. You said ten thousand ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just find it first. Could you assist, ten thousand ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which line would you like to take me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can pull up here, Mr. President. Line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read a small portion of his statement that was shown to the witness which is not in evidence. It was an Official Note compiled on the 13th of October, and it relates to the Grubori situation. It describes what you reportedly have said as follows. What I did is I put to that witness at that time what was reported what he had said, and then I asked him whether that reflected what he stated, which is, of course, something totally different from putting to this witness a statement given by another person. It's incomparable, and I would like to you strictly adhere to the guidance I gave before. We're not going to compare every -- we have now carefully compared what you are doing at this moment to what I did at that moment. If you want to ask the witness whether -- if this is a statement given by him, and if you want to ask him whether this document reflects what is he said, something which I allowed you to do with the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem with that. I allowed to you do that. This, however, is a totally different situation. If you have any questions in relation to this document, first, put them to the witness, and if then it would turn out to be useful to put this document to the witness after he has answered the questions, you may do so, but not to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I may just supplement that, Your Honour, if I can -- Your Honour, I can also look at 9931 where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm not doing -- I gave you my clear guidance, and I want you to adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like is us be treated the same way the Prosecution was when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it is it clear that, of course, you insist, and rightly so, to be treated in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you put me with quite a strong voice, Look there, and we find something which is, first of all, not something the Prosecution did; what I did. Second, it's different from what you are doing now, and I don't want to spend, at this moment, any further time on it. You have received my guidance. Please proceed in the way I asked you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that Mr. Rasic had given a statement to the police in the 12th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we take the document from the screen, of course, Mr. Kehoe is entitled to ask whether this witness is aware of any statement given.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But then the next is obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question, we'll see, Mr. Hedaraly. Let's not anticipate on what will be the next question. I think Mr. Kehoe has fairly well understood what he is expected to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware of that, Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, once I was released from the prison, after nine months, that the two of them, Zec and Jakovljevic had been detained two days before we were, and that they were interrogated. After I left the prison, I heard that Ivica Koljevic went to Tribun [phoen] to see Zec and that they had a fight, a brawl. I don't know what the reason was, but I was always interested in knowing why the police brought me in, following what, and then I learned that the two of them had been interviewed before. And then, I suppose, that they may have said something which was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Were you aware that Mr. Rasic told the police that you were present when Petric killed this man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean the witness's answer was clear, so now is he impeaching his own witness? Is he trying to confront --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. I'm confronting him with inconsistent information coming from other individuals which were entitled to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is aware, apparently, that at least he heard that a statement was taken. Did you ever see that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never. That was after we were released from prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did ... let me just check one second. Now, do you know anything about whether, when Mr. Rasic gave his statement, whether he told the truth, or did you ever receive any information that he did or did not tell the truth when that statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear here for the first time that he said I was present at the place of the murder. I didn't know that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware at all about the content of the statement he gave at the time? Apart from what you heard here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the two days before we were brought in? When they had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was, whether you learned about what was written down as his statement any earlier than this week.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the trial, I heard what he said in his interview. But this part, in which he said that I was at the place where Canak was murdered, there was no such discussion in the courtroom. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were aware of the content of his statement from what you learned at this trial but not that he would have said that you were present during the murder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer 1D2727 into evidence as a bar table submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we'll object to that, Your Honour. Mr. Rasic is a witness on the Defence witness list that we have been told would not be called, so this is an attempt to -- to -- to backdoor evidence. This very chamber, twice, did not accept such statements. Once happened when Mr. Cayley objected to witness 70 as an Official Note about the Grubori investigation of one of the witnesses the Prosecution has dropped, and therefore the Prosecution withdrew that note. There was also the incident with Mr. Hjertnes, and if the Chamber remembers, there was a report Mr. Hayden testified to. There was a reference to Mr. Hjertnes, what he had said, and that was redacted because the Prosecution had dropped him from its witness list. And the Chamber essentially said that we should not be allowed to, therefore, backdoor evidence of a witness that it had dropped. If the Gotovina intends to call Mr. Rasic, then we can MFI the note until he comes to testify. Informally, we were told he would not be testifying. If that has changed, then we can MFI it. But if he is not coming, then it should not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Hedaraly knows full well why the -- I know why the Prosecution is objecting, but they know the full reason why the Defence is overing these. If we can go back, and I can cite to you during their opening statement, their pre-trial brief, and any number of instances during the trial where the argument the by the Prosecution was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you please would slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. My apologies. The argument was that crimes were committed, and, essentially, the Croatian authorities did nothing. All of these records go directly to that particular issue. Now, with regard to this, and we will have others on that score, where they admitted where these notes are going to reflect that in fact that took place. That there were investigations, that there were prosecutions, that there were people being interviewed, that the authorities did doing something, that they were acting in concert. Whether or not they did it well or not, that can be waived by the Trial Chamber. But certainly in the face of the allegations of the Prosecution during their case, this objection by counsel is misplaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd, and both parties are invited to make a very brief submissions, I would say, content, 3, 400 words, pointing at similar situations, pointing at differences, because, Mr. Hedaraly, it may be clear that Mr. Kehoe apparently, although that may not have transpired immediately very clear, but apparently is seeking admission of this document to show the investigatorial activities, rather than the truth of the content. Both parties can make a one A4, 3 to 400-words submission. Mr. Registrar, the document will be MFI'd under number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1540, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1540 keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could turn to 1D2732.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as this is coming up, Mr. Perkovic, with regard to this killing, were you aware that Mr. Mijic, Zuki was interviewed concerning this matter by the police in 16 October 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you we are now -- of course I'm interested, are we now talking about the content, about the substance of it? Because that is it how we started with the last document, and we ended up in a totally different area, it was not content but, rather, investigative activities. I'd like to know, do you want to -- to invite the witness to comment on investigative activities, or about content or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this instance, it's both. Was he aware, and then with regard to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think last time, I asked you not to have it on the screen when we start putting questions to the witness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the -- and I didn't put it on the screen. It's actually for Your Honours' purposes. I didn't put the area that we are talking about which is the last page, and I did that purposely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please ask the witness, and then we'll have on the screen once we need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Zuki was questioned about this incident?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew he was detained and that he was questioned about the case during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you ever learn that Zuki told the police that Petric was angry at the old man because he had not told him about these weapons? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say you learned that during the proceedings, you learned that at trial?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware that a Mile Hrustic was at Zrmanja when this killing took place? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: When we were returning from the old man, we encountered two of them moving in his direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So they were moving -- I'm sorry, just by way of clarification. Are you saying that, When we were returning from the old man, we encountered two of them -- two individuals moving in the direction of the old man? I'm just trying to get clarification of your answer.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were moving in his direction. He was angry, asking about how come he gave us the rifle, whereas he had not given it to him, and then they left. We didn't follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, can you give us the identity. You just said, "they were moving in the direction. He was angry asking about how come he gave us the rifle, whereas he had not given it to him." Who is that "he"?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Petric, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the other person -- was the other person moving -- who was the other person that was moving in the direction of the old man with Hrustic?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: The other person was Hrustic; he was with Petric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 1D2732. And in support of this application, as opposed to an MFI, Your Honour, I would of course MFI it at this point, but I ask the Court to consider its decision of 30 January 2009 as a basis for the admission of the MUP statements into evidence. But we can address that at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The objection is identical. It's another witness that will not be called. Just for the record, Your Honour, the witness answered the question. There was no need to show him that this other person said he was angry. The witness, when asked himself, did -- and that is essentially what we think should happen. But for the record, the objection is the same, and it is going to be covered in the same submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- you will understand, Mr. Kehoe. That the 30th of January is not something which immediately brings back to my mind the exact line, how we decided the matter. Could you please include this in any submissions. You get five extra lines for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So may go up to 450 words. The document, meanwhile, being MFI'd. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1541, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed. Could the Chamber receive the submissions by, let say, by the end of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want me to continue on or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's time for a break. Could you tell us how much more time you would after the break, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's my information that the witness was scheduled for one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was, Mr. President, and I ask for Your Honours' indulgence in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar is retrieving the information, I have to correct myself. You may have noticed that was a bit hesitant in the beginning as far as P2550 was concerned. The issue was not admission because there is still an objection which needs to be decided. The issue at this moment was whether it should remain under seal. For the time being, it should. But where I said that it is admitted under seal, I was anticipating on what may or may not happen, but that was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me also add a second objection, which I didn't do when you give the initial ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is withdraw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will object on equality of arms grounds. I'm assuming that the reason it's under seal is because the matter -- the subpoena is confidential in the other proceeding. And if -- or under seal in the other proceeding. If that is the case, the Prosecution should not be allowed to use materials for which it, exclusively in these proceedings, has access and for which the Defence would not be able to obtain access to other documents that may be relevant to that issue that may also be under seal. Again that presupposes that the subpoena is non-public, and therefore it is something that only the Prosecution would be able to retrieve in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there would have been a request to have access to confidential material in other proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in this particular case, we would have had no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- clue to go to the Blaskic proceeding and then start examining subpoena issues in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that document was tendered, and therefore shown to the Defence, so they have had a chance to review it, and therefore they can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the issue is that the Defence has no access to confidential materials in other cases, so they can't make a selection, as, apparently, you were able to do, because you, apparently, had knowledge of confidential documents in other cases from your colleagues. Or -- I don't take it, it was yourself in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was not at that, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I see the point. And I guess what -- is that the Defence is free to make such a request [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, but then you also know that the case law does not allow fishing expeditions in that respect. Give me whatever could be relevant from all cases; that's the issue. Give it some thought, and we'd like to hear the position of the Prosecution after these thoughts have been developed within the next two days, I would say. Then we'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just give me one second. Mr. Kehoe, you used, until now, a little bit over one hour. If you could try to really finish within the next hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will. I give -- quote my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just without blowing up, I am referring to 1D2731. And with regard to this same killing, sir, Mr. Perkovic, were you aware that Mr. Hrustic gave a statement to the police in October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Mr. Hrustic or Rasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hrustic.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was interrogated, just as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Hrustic picked Mr. Petric out of a -- or picked out a photo of Mr. Petric out as the killer of Mr. Canak?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Whose photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The individual who was killed.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. This wasn't something that happened at trial, that he indicated a photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The photo I'm talking about is Petric's photo. Were you aware that Mr. Hrustic picked out Mr. Petric's photo as the killer of Mr. Canak?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that, during the trial, he stated that Petric had killed Mr. Canak. I know that Hrustic stated that he fired a shot past the old man, whereas Petric shot the old man. Petric, on the other hand, claimed quite the opposite, but it was Petric who was ultimately convicted by the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As bar-table submission, Your Honour, we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2731 consistent with Your Honours' prior rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Part of the same submission, then, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for my information, Mr. Kehoe, you asked the selection of a photograph of Mr. Petric. Have I misunderstood the testimony until now, that Mr. Petric and Mr. Hrustic knew each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, selection of a photograph is whether you say Mr. Petric or where you point at the photograph is -- is from my understanding of photo spreads, identification procedures is totally irrelevant, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not really, Judge. I think it is probably very pertinent. I mean the photo spreads that you know about where police officers do, you know, recognise the individual who killed Mr. Canak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you know him now -- if they give me five photographs of all Defence counsel, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I hope you don't pick me. Pick Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But the value, the identification value is close to zero if you know the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Judge. I mean obviously -- I can tell you a perfect example -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... The perfect example is, let's say you're doing an investigation, and you do a photo spread. And for some reason, heaven knows why, the witness who picked him out in a photo spread, police somehow deceases. Can you as a police officer then come in and say, I showed a photograph to Mr. X, and he identified this individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you give the name, if you know the person, then it is totally superfluous. That's what I understand -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... But let's not engage in this very interesting discussion, as I cut off some other discussions throughout this morning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, Your Honours, I just offered that item consistent with Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be MFI'd. Mr. Registrar, that will be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1542, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for every additional document, 25 more words. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, in addition to this killing of Mr. Canak, did the police also ask you, and I believe you touched on it this morning, about the incident where this man's feet were burnt, in Zrmanja?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. And what did you tell the police happened on that event?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which person you're referring to. To the person we referred to earlier on, or to Canak? I described Zec setting some rags on fire that were placed beneath the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the individual, not Mr. Canak who was killed, but the man who lived.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that they tied up the man. I don't know if it was Petric or Zec who tied him up -- or, rather, I know that for a fact that Zec tied him up. I'm not sure if Petric was involved. I know that they placed some rags beneath the old man and set them on fire. Subsequently, they put the fire out by stamping it with their feet. It was no big fire, just to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to D1539, your first statement, and turn to page 5 in the English, and I will check the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes, there are two incidents, fires. Could you make sure the witness knows -- there's one on page 4 and page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The witness says this is the individual who is alive. I think that's what we clarified -- the other one is dead. If we can go to the last page in the English and the second-to-last page in the B/C/S. And it notes at the top of the page: "Three days after this, Zec, Petric and he ," this is your statement to the police, "went to another old man in Zrmanja. The old man was about 170 to 180 centimetres tall, skinny, about 65 to 70 years of age, had grey hair and slightly balding. Petric and Zec asked the old man for weapons, and when the old man told them that he did not have a rifle, Zec and Petric tied him with wire to a tree in the yard next to the house. They gagged him with a rag, threw some rags around the old man's feet and set them on fire. Pero said that at that time he had gone behind the house so he would not have to watch this. He told them to let the old man go."

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what happened with Canak, the person who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So in the incident where the individual lived, did a similar sequence of events take place, where Zec and Petric burned the man's feet?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Petric, but I do know about Zec. I know that it was on the patio of the old man's house where they tied him up to the railing. I don't recall if Lasan was with us. I know that they tied him up, and they placed these rags under his him, just as they did in the other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you saw them do that, sir, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that the old man was suffering, and I told them to untie him. Then the old man took us to the place where the rifle was so that he could give it to us.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the events we talked about in Cakici and Zrmanja, were you also investigated for killings that took place in Gosici?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a suspect in relation to Gosici. I was the subject of an investigation that went on for nine months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that is perfect. I gave the relevant instructions to Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Perkovic, if we can turn our attention to 1D2725, your second statement, or second Official Note to the police, 17 October 1995. Now, Mr. Perkovic, this second statement, did you give this statement to -- or this information to the police on the 17th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever I stated to the police was the result of their mistreatment of me. We were being interrogated day and night and another day. We were beaten, brain-washed, and such-like. I said certain things that had nothing to do with the situation on the style -- on the ground, as the reconstruction took place with the participation of the investigating magistrate at the scene of crime, they realized that they had nothing -- whatever I stated, did not reflect the situation on the ground, because I mentioned certain high-rise buildings, several-storey buildings which did not exist on the ground. When the reconstruction of the crime took place, we attended the scene in the village of Gosici, and one was able to see that these were one-storey family houses there. When I was being interrogated, I was out of sorts, I was mistreated, and I told the investigating judge as much. You could see by reading my statement that I had never in fact been to Gosici. Later on, as the trial progressed, I told the judge where it was that I was present, indeed, on the ground, in which village.
