utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm just reminded, I did not tender 65 ter 7312, the testimony of the platoon commander. Before I forget, if we could do that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2560, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you see any other instances of soldiers burning houses, other than the ones in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: On my way through the village of Zrmanja, I saw houses that were burned. Quite a few civilians went into the village and looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go -- just go back briefly to the statement you gave to the investigative judge on 17 October; that is P2556. And it is at page 5 of the English. It's is at page 4 of the B/C/S, at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, and at the bottom as well in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you say, talking about some of the people that may have been killed, the last sentence said: "It was normal to come to a village and shoot around." Can you explain to the Court what you meant by that statement.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: These were certain individuals who, like, for instance, Radovic, would just go into a village and open fire. I didn't consider that individual to be any serious sort of person, this Radovic. He merely opened fire on the roofs on the walls of buildings. The intention wasn't to frighten any civilians who may have been there, but simply wilfully opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interests of time, I'll conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Witness, I have some -- several questions for you. The first I wanted to know approximately distance from your -- I'm saying it's Vodice, your place where you are living, yeah, and this -- and place where your units were dispatched at that time. How long a distance it was? When you mentioned you travelling through different villages encountered in Google Maps, there was approximately 93 kilometres. Is it correct, or it's -- it's not?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the distance to Zrmanja or to Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to Zrmanja where your unit was located.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the distance in kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Which means every day you were travelling back from Zrmanja to Vodice to spend the night?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We engaged in sweeping terrain only during the day. It was only for a short period of time that we -- some of us slept in the village of Rudele, while others still went home. We would be sweeping the terrain in the direction of Zrmanja during the day and go home to spend the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: How was organised this chain of command in your regiment, if you were allowed to freely to go to home and back, and there was no control at all?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: There was control. The commander saw that he need not keep all the soldiers on the ground all the time. Soldiers were tired, and so he instructed them to spend nights at home. It was only elements of these men that spent nights in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Did you travel by personal vehicles, or do you have some service cars?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Both. Military vehicles and civilian vehicles were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And, for instance, during operation -- during operation, you withdraw some sort of weapons. How do you be -- treat with these weapons? Did you submit these weapons to -- to your superior, and you should sign some documents that you receive? Or is it just voluntary matter?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons that were found were not officially handed over. People who found weapons kept them. But to tell you the truth, I don't remember anymore whether the weapons were handed over or not. As for our personal side-arms that we were issued with, we would take those home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And what happened with those weapons, afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Quite a few individuals who had these weapons at home handed them over to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. You told us that you returned on the 7th of August, and that a general shouted at soldiers, What kind of soldiers you are, looting? And you told us that you passed several check-points. Do you remember check-points were manned by police, military police, the military? Could you tell us who manned those check-points.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Check-points were manned by both the civilian and military police, and I mean all the more important check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us how many check-points approximately you passed, because you came from Kistanje, you went to Vodice, which is a distance of some 35 kilometres. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three check-points, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two or three check-points. And both civilian and military. And you said there was no hindrance in passing those check-points; you would just let through, is that --

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you describe what kind of goods were on the truck.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Cement mixer, TV set, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, I think the answer at line 25, perhaps needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I said you would just be let through, and that is what is in line. Is there any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Now, you told this general shouted at these soldiers. Was it -- what kind of general was it? Do you know more specifics about --

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him. I was just about to pass water, and he yelled and went on about his business. It was -- it took a minute, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you didn't see him. How did you know that the person yelling was a general, if you didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the others ones told me so. I heard some sort of racket and then I asked what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did the others tell you whether this was a -- was it a HV general, or was it a ...

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's what they told you. You were a member of the 15th Home Guard Regiment, and you told us that you had to sign for your resignation when you were arrested. Had you been on active duty on, from the beginning from Operation Oluja?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout. I didn't even know when I was signing the paper what it was I signed. When I signed it, they told me, As of this moment, you are no longer a Croatian soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you had no been demobilized before that date; that is, before the 16th or 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. I was out in the field at Ostrelj in Bosnia. When I came back from Ostrelj, they took me into custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us about the nickname that was suggested to you, if I may so, by the police when you gave your statement, the nickname Matilda. Did never anyone called you Pero Matilda, or Matilda?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. They called me Matilda. I told you that I didn't have a nickname of any sort. And then they said, Well, since you own this bar, Matilda, we'll call you Matilda. So whenever there was a mention of Pero, then everybody would ask, Which Pero? And they say, Pero Matilda. That's how they knew me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I understand you that this was invented only on the day when you were interviewed by the police, that then they came up with this suggestion and that -- or would there have been other peoples who would have called you Matilda at any earlier date?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose they did call me Matilda. They'd call me Pero, and then if somebody didn't know which Pero they referred to, they would say Matilda. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was prior to giving this statement to the police. You were aware that if Pero was not clear enough, that they would call you Pero Matilda.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: They wouldn't say Pero Matilda. They would say Pero from Matilda, meaning the bar. That's how they would know me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was named after your mother, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I know. Yes, yes, her name is Matilda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, Judge Kinis asked you - this was at page 95, line 20. Judge Kinis asked - excuse me, line 18 is the question - "did you travel by personal vehicles, or did you have some service cars?" And your answer was: "Both. Military vehicles and civilian vehicles were used." Sorry. Now, after Operation Storm, what did you drive around in? A military vehicle or a civilian vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: There were military and civilian ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And which was the civilian vehicle that you travelled around in?

utterances.speaker: PERO PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I would sometimes use the Zastava that I took, and at other times I would take the military van we were issued with, Though I used the van more frequently than the Zastava car which you drove around Vodice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had -- I must admit that I had it on my mind, a question which is to some extent related, Mr. Kehoe. This statement you gave on the 16th of October talks about the Zastava. Now you told us that it was an abandoned car today, which you took. Where did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was around the village of Rudele, when we were out in the field. I think it was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was it on the a road? Was it in a field? Was it in a yard of a house? Was it on a parking lot? Where did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: {Interpretation] In the yard of a house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what made you believe that a car found in a yard of a house is an abandoned car? Apparently no one was sitting in it. But what made you believe on that -- in those early stages that it was an abandoned car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there were no civilians around. This was just one of the many abandoned vehicles. Since I didn't have a car of my own and I needed one to move about Vodice, I took it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know who was living in that house in which -- in the yard of which you found this car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it a civilian house? I mean, was the house such that you would expect civilians to live in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who lived in it. It must have been civilians. Who else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... an ordinary house where you would find a family --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was a village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What did you finally do with the car? Did you keep it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kept it, until the police took it. And I think they took it before I was detained. Because it didn't have a licence plate. It had not been registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Had you taken it off, the licence plate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't have any plates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have my questions triggered any further need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Perkovic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answers you've given on questions put to you both by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let me first briefly deal with one matter, and I'd like to turn into private session for a second for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, briefly, please, because I know already with which of my colleagues I will have problems this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, P2559 was MFI'd. We have no objection to its admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P2559 is admitted into evidence. I finally put on the record, I think, that we have some six documents which are part of the cluster for which we started. We have 3 to 400 words, and I leave it to you to add the 25 for all the next, and we would like to receive submissions in relation to that by the end of this week. If there is no other matter, we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, 1st of July, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
